body.statement: The map \(F_6\) has a unique zero \(s_6\) in the stated rational interval; all four weights \(A_6B_6\), \(B_6\), \(C_6B_6\), and \(D_6B_6\) are positive. The seven-state prior \(\pi_6\) makes \(g_6(W)\) the full-count posterior mean on every cell of positive predictive mass. The seven support-state risks equal \(s_6^2\), and each of the other \(77\) states has risk strictly below \(s_6^2\). Hence \[\rho_6^{\mathrm{CR}}=\rho_6^W=s_6^2.\]
body.justification: The algebraic seven-state saddle is the nontrivial equality certificate needed to make eight the first failure rather than merely an example of failure.
body.gap: Hull reports numerical complete-randomization evidence and Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen solve an independent-assignment scalar game; neither supplies this hypergeometric saddle or its \(77\) inactive inequalities.
body.consumer: Finite-game solvers gain an exact algebraic benchmark that detects false strictness caused by arbitrary actions on prior-null cells.
body.proof_tex:
Write \(s=s_6\), \(u=u_6\), \(v=v_6\), and \(z=z_6\).  We first certify the algebraic quantities.  Let
\[
 s_-:=\frac{29066256529188}{10^{14}},\qquad
 s_+:=\frac{29066256529190}{10^{14}}.
\]
On this interval \(s>29/100\), and hence
\[
 9s^2+2s-1>9\left(\frac{29}{100}\right)^2+\frac{58}{100}-1
 =\frac{3369}{10000}>0.
\]
Thus \(F_6\) is continuous there.  Put \(H=10^{30}\).  For a positive rational \(r\), use
\[
 \frac{\lfloor H\sqrt r\rfloor}{H}
 \leq\sqrt r<
 \frac{\lfloor H\sqrt r\rfloor+1}{H},
\]
with each floor verified by the two adjacent integer-square comparisons.  In the three instances needed here, those verified floors are
\[
\begin{array}{c|r}
r&\lfloor H\sqrt r\rfloor\\ \hline
10&3162277660168379331998893544432\\
9s_-^2+2s_--1&584540565181123795260932473001\\
9s_+^2+2s_+-1&584540565181247515095038637970.
\end{array}
\]
Because the two radical coefficients in \(F_6\) are negative, substitution of the upper radical endpoints in the first case and the lower radical endpoints in the second gives, by integer cross-multiplication,
\[
\begin{aligned}
F_6(s_-)&\geq \frac35s_-^2-\frac4{15}\frac{3162277660168379331998893544433}{H}s_-
-\frac2{15}s_--\frac2{15}\frac{584540565181123795260932473002}{H}+\frac{14}{45}
>10^{-14},\\
F_6(s_+)&\leq \frac35s_+^2-\frac4{15}\frac{3162277660168379331998893544432}{H}s_+
-\frac2{15}s_+-\frac2{15}\frac{584540565181247515095038637970}{H}+\frac{14}{45}
<-10^{-14}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the endpoint signs are exact rational inequalities, not floating-point evaluations.  Moreover, throughout the interval, using \(s<3/10\), \(\sqrt{10}>3\), and positivity of the radical term,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 F_6'(s)
 &=\frac{6s}{5}-\frac{4\sqrt{10}}{15}-\frac2{15}
   -\frac{2(9s+1)}{15\sqrt{9s^2+2s-1}}\\
 &<\frac9{25}-\frac{12}{15}-\frac2{15}
 =-\frac{43}{75}<0.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The intermediate value theorem and strict monotonicity therefore give one and only one zero \(s\in(s_-,s_+)\).

The same exact integer-square comparisons give the convenient rational enclosure
\[
 \frac{19484685506037}{10^{14}}<u<\frac{19484685506042}{10^{14}},
 \qquad
 \frac{45957786843487}{10^{14}}<v<\frac{45957786843491}{10^{14}}.
\]
In particular \(0<u<2/3\), \(0<v<2/3\), and \(z=1-s>2/3\).  Consequently
\[
 D_6=\frac{2-3u}{9u}>0,qquad
 C_6=\frac2{3v}-1>0,qquad
 A_6=\frac{(3z-2)+zD_6}{10(1-z)}>0,
\]
and \(B_6=(1+A_6+C_6+D_6)^{-1}>0\).  The seven displayed prior masses are therefore positive, and their sum is
\[
 A_6B_6+B_6+C_6B_6+D_6B_6=1.
\]

We next verify the four support-orbit risks from the hypergeometric coefficients.  For the representatives in the first column, the nonzero kernel entries and the resulting risks are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
N&\{(x,y):K_N(x,y)\}&R_N^W(g_6)\\ \hline
(0,6,0,0)&\{(3,0):1\}&(1-z)^2=s^2\\
(1,4,0,1)&\{(2,0):1/5,(2,1):3/10,(3,0):3/10,(3,1):1/5\}
&\frac25(v-\frac23)^2+\frac3{10}(u-\frac23)^2+\frac3{10}(z-\frac23)^2\\
(2,0,0,4)&\{(1,3):1/5,(2,2):3/5,(3,1):1/5\}&\frac25v^2=s^2\\
(3,0,0,3)&\{(0,3):1/20,(1,2):9/20,(2,1):9/20,(3,0):1/20\}
&\frac1{10}z^2+\frac9{10}u^2=s^2.
\end{array}
\]
Indeed, the definitions give
\[
 u^2=s^2+\frac{2s}{9}-\frac19,qquad
 v^2=\frac52s^2,qquad z=1-s.
\]
These identities prove the first, third, and fourth risk equalities.  After their substitution, the second risk minus \(s^2\) is
\[
 \frac35s^2-\frac8{15}v-\frac2{15}s-\frac25u+\frac{14}{45}
 =F_6(s)=0.
\]
Arm exchange supplies the reflected partners, so all seven support-state risks equal \(s^2\).

Here is an exhaustive exact check of the inactive states.  Expanding Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}hypergeometric\mbox{-}kernel}\), and then replacing \(u^2\) and \(v^2\) by the two identities above, gives the following complete multiset of risks for the \(77\) states outside the support.  The representative merely labels each collected algebraic value; the multiplicities sum to \(77\).
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|l}
\text{representative }N&\text{multiplicity}&R_N^W(g_6)\\ \hline
(0,0,5,1)&4&\frac74s^2-\frac16s-\frac56v+\frac{13}{36}\\
(1,0,3,2)&4&\frac{11}{8}s^2-\frac{13}{180}s-\frac7{20}u-\frac7{20}v+\frac{19}{90}\\
(2,0,1,3)&4&s^2+\frac1{60}s-\frac1{20}u-\frac1{30}v+\frac1{90}\\
(2,0,2,2)&2&\frac{11}{10}s^2-\frac1{45}s-\frac15u-\frac2{15}v+\frac4{45}\\
(0,0,4,2)&4&\frac{19}{10}s^2-\frac4{45}s-\frac4{15}u-\frac45v+\frac{16}{45}\\
(1,0,2,3)&4&\frac{23}{20}s^2+\frac1{90}s-\frac16u-\frac15v+\frac4{45}\\
(2,1,1,2)&1&\frac9{10}s^2+\frac4{45}s-\frac2{45}\\
(0,0,3,3)&4&\frac{13}{8}s^2+\frac1{20}s-\frac9{20}u-\frac9{20}v+\frac15\\
(1,0,1,4)&4&s^2+\frac19s-\frac1{30}u-\frac1{15}v-\frac1{36}\\
(0,1,4,1)&4&\frac74s^2+\frac19s-\frac12u-\frac12v+\frac7{36}\\
(1,1,3,1)&2&\frac{23}{20}s^2+\frac4{45}s-\frac4{15}u-\frac15v+\frac1{15}\\
(1,1,1,3)&2&\frac{17}{20}s^2+\frac2{15}s-\frac1{15}\\
(0,1,5,0)&2&\frac52s^2-\frac43v+\frac49\\
(1,1,2,2)&4&\frac78s^2+\frac19s-\frac1{15}u-\frac1{20}v-\frac1{36}\\
(1,0,0,5)&2&s^2+\frac29s-\frac19\\
(0,0,2,4)&8&\frac{11}{10}s^2+\frac2{15}s-\frac25u-\frac2{15}v+\frac2{45}\\
(0,1,2,3)&4&\frac58s^2+\frac19s-\frac2{15}u-\frac1{60}v-\frac1{36}\\
(1,2,2,1)&1&\frac35s^2+\frac2{15}s-\frac1{15}\\
(0,2,4,0)&2&s^2+\frac29s-\frac23u\\
(0,1,1,4)&4&\frac25s^2+\frac4{45}s-\frac2{45}\\
(0,0,1,5)&8&\frac12s^2+\frac19s-\frac16u-\frac1{36}\\
(0,0,0,6)&3&0.
\end{array}
\]
Applying ordinary outward interval arithmetic to these \(22\) displayed affine expressions on the three rational enclosures above, the smallest lower endpoint of \(s^2-R_N^W(g_6)\) is
\[
 \frac{625559548802811553841070521}
 {90000000000000000000000000000}>\frac{69}{10000}>0.
\]
All operations in this last display are rational additions and multiplications; the radical membership in the boxes was already certified by integer squaring.  This proves all \(77\) strict inequalities and, together with the support calculation, proves
\[
 \max_{N\in\mathcal N_6}R_N^W(g_6)=s^2.
\]

It remains to certify that the same prior is dual-feasible for the full-count experiment.  The common positive factor \(B_6\) cancels from posterior means.  For positive differences \(x-y\), the only positive-predictive-mass cells and their posterior means are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{cells}&\mathbb E_{\pi_6}(\tau_N\mid X_1=x,X_0=y)\\ \hline
(2,0),(3,1)&\displaystyle\frac{2}{3(1+C_6)}=v\\[3pt]
(2,1)&\displaystyle\frac{1/10}{3/20+9D_6/20}=u\\[3pt]
(3,0)&\displaystyle\frac{A_6/2+1/10}{A_6/2+3/20+D_6/20}=z.
\end{array}
\]
The first equality is equivalent to \(1+C_6=2/(3v)\), the second to \(3+9D_6=2/u\), and the third to
\[
 10A_6(1-z)=3z+zD_6-2;
\]
these are exactly the definitions of \(C_6,D_6,A_6\).  The two zero-difference cells \((1,1),(2,2)\) receive mass only from zero-effect states and hence have posterior mean zero.  Arm-exchange symmetry supplies the negative-difference cells.  Therefore the full-count posterior mean on every positive-predictive-mass cell is \(g_6(2x-2y)\).

The Bayes risk of \(\pi_6\) under full counts is consequently the prior average of the seven support risks, namely \(s^2\).  The dual lower bound, the information inequality, and the scalar primal upper bound now form the chain
\[
 s^2\leq\rho_6^{\mathrm{CR}}\leq\rho_6^W\leq s^2.
\]
This proves the asserted saddle and equality.
